text: Reza Aslan (Persian: رضا اصلان, IPA: [ˈɾezɒː æsˈlɒːn]; born May 3, 1972) is an Iranian-American scholar of sociology, writer, and television host. Born into a Twelver Shia Muslim family, he converted to evangelical Christianity at age 15 and reverted to Islam the summer before attending Harvard, where he completed his degree in 1999. Aslan holds a B.A. in religious studies from Santa Clara University, a Master of Theological Studies (MTS) from Harvard Divinity School, a Master of Fine Arts (M.F.A.) in fiction writing from the University of Iowa's Writers' Workshop, and a Ph.D. in sociology from the University of California, Santa Barbara. His 2009 dissertation, "Global Jihadism as a Transnational Social Movement: A Theoretical Framework," discusses contemporary Muslim political activism. Aslan has written four books: No God but God: The Origins, Evolution, and Future of Islam (2005), How to Win a Cosmic War: God, Globalization, and the End of Terror (2009), re-released in 2010 as Beyond Fundamentalism: Confronting Religious Extremism in the Age of Globalization, Zealot: The Life and Times of Jesus of Nazareth (2013), and An American Martyr in Persia: The Epic Life and Tragic Death of Howard Baskerville (2022). He has also edited two anthologies: Tablet and Pen: Literary Landscapes from the Modern Middle East (2011) and Muslims and Jews in America: Commonalities, Contentions, and Complexities (2011). Aslan has written for numerous media outlets, including The Daily Beast, The Los Angeles Times, The New York Times, The Washington Post, Slate, The Boston Globe, The Guardian, The Nation, and The Christian Science Monitor. He is a professor of creative writing at the University of California, Riverside, and a board member of the National Iranian American Council (NIAC). Aslan's family fled Iran in 1979 and settled in the San Francisco Bay Area; he attended Del Mar High School in San Jose and graduated in 1990. In the early 1990s, he taught at De La Salle High School in Concord, California. He served as a visiting faculty member in Islamic and Middle Eastern Studies at the University of Iowa in August 2000 while at the Iowa Writers' Workshop and was the 2012–13 Wallerstein Distinguished Visiting Professor at the Drew University Center on Religion, Culture & Conflict. He is an Adjunct Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations from 2012 to 2013, a member of the Los Angeles Institute for the Humanities and the Pacific Council on International Policy, and serves on the boards of the Ploughshares Fund, PEN Center USA, The Markaz, the Chicago Theological Seminary, and the Yale Humanist Community. Aslan founded Aslan Media and partnered with Mahyad Tousi to create BoomGen Studios in 2006, which produced projects such as National Geographic's Amreeka, Disney's Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, the Broadway adaptation of Aladdin, Miral, Desert Dancer, The Trials of Spring, Rosewater, and The Square. In January 2015, ABC picked up Of Kings and Prophets, a biblical epic produced by Aslan, Tousi, and Jason Reed, which followed the story of King David and was set in the Kingdom of Israel but filmed in Cape Town, South Africa. Aslan joined HBO's The Leftovers as a consulting producer for its second and third seasons, playing a key role in shaping protagonist Kevin Garvey's character arc. In March 2016, Ovation premiered Rough Draft with Reza Aslan, a talk show featuring Aslan discussing topics with authors and writers. In 2015, Aslan began production on the documentary series Believer, which follows his immersive experiences with various religious traditions, focusing on fringe sects. The first episode featured the Aghori sect of Hinduism, where Aslan ate part of a human brain, leading to accusations of sensationalism and anti-Hinduism. Critics, including the United States India Political Action Committee, Vamsee Juluri, Aseem Shukla, and US Congresswoman Tulsi Gabbard, condemned the episode for misrepresenting Hinduism, calling it racist, anti-immigrant, and inaccurate. Aslan claimed he had planned to cover the Ashura festival in Pakistan but abandoned it due to insurance costs and pledged to cover Islam if a second season of Believer were produced. On June 9, 2017, CNN announced it would not proceed with a second season of Believer after Aslan's anti-Trump tweets were criticized for using vulgar language. Aslan defended the episode in a Facebook post and stated he is not a journalist but a social commentator and scholar, agreeing with CNN that it was best to part ways. Aslan also wrote a sitcom pilot titled "Allah in the Family" based on his experiences as an Iranian immigrant in Oklahoma, which ABC bought but has not yet produced. After the 2017 London Bridge attack, Aslan criticized President Donald Trump on Twitter, calling him "a piece of shit" and a "man-baby," leading to CNN's decision to end their collaboration. Aslan has made numerous media appearances on NPR, Fox News, PBS, The Rachel Maddow Show, Meet the Press, The Daily Show, The Colbert Report, Anderson Cooper 360°, Hardball, Nightline, Real Time with Bill Maher, Fareed Zakaria GPS, and ABC Australia's Big Ideas. In a 2013 Fox News interview, Aslan defended his right to write about Jesus as a scholar of religion, despite criticism from Fox host Lauren Green, who questioned his credentials. The interview went viral and boosted sales of Zealot, which reached number four on The New York Times best-seller list and topped Amazon's U.S. list by late July 2013. Academic scholars, including Elizabeth Castelli of Barnard College and Manuel Roig-Franzia of The Washington Post, criticized Aslan's claims of being a historian, noting that his university does not offer degrees in the history or sociology of religion, though his dissertation adviser, Mark Juergensmeyer, acknowledged that Aslan completed most of his coursework in religion and was placed in sociology to avoid language requirements. Aslan is a sitting member of the advisory board for the National Iranian American Council and, in 2015, co-signed with 73 other Middle East scholars a statement supporting the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. Aslan refers to Al Qaeda's jihad against the West as "a cosmic war," distinct from holy war, in which rival religious groups are engaged in an earthly battle for material goals, and he argues that American rhetoric of "war on terrorism" mirrors this cosmic dualism. He distinguishes between Islamism and Jihadism, asserting that Islamists have legitimate goals and can be negotiated with, while Jihadists seek a pan-Islamic, borderless religious communalism. Aslan's solution to the cosmic war is to engage moderate Islamic political forces in democratic processes, noting that such participation has reduced support for extremist groups. The New Yorker called Beyond Fundamentalism a "thoughtful analysis of America's War on Terror," and The Washington Post described it as offering a "very persuasive argument for the best way to counter jihadism." In Zealot, Aslan presents Jesus as a political, rebellious, and eschatological Jew who called for regime change to end Roman hegemony and oppressive religious leadership. In a 2013 interview with WNYC, Aslan stated that all religions are languages of symbols and metaphors to express faith, and in a 2014 interview with Cenk Uygur, he described Islam as a man-made institution composed of symbols and metaphors that provide a language for the inexpressible, not more right or wrong than other religions. Kirkus Reviews called An American Martyr in Persia "an intriguing read that breathes life into a pivotal moment of Persian/Iranian history."

Aslan is a professor of creative writing at the University of California, Riverside and a board member of the National Iranian American Council (NIAC), serving as a sitting member of its advisory board. In 2015, as part of the group, he signed a statement of support for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action alongside 73 other prominent International Relations and Middle East scholars. He describes Al Qaeda's jihad against the West as a "cosmic war," distinct from holy war, which he views as a ritual drama reflecting a battle occurring in the heavens, contrasting with American rhetoric of a "war on terrorism" that operates within the same structure of "cosmic dualism." Aslan distinguishes between Islamism and Jihadism, asserting that Islamists have legitimate goals and can be negotiated with, whereas Jihadists seek an idealized, pan-Islamic, borderless "religious communalism" and are not open to dialogue. His solution to the cosmic war is engagement with moderate Islamic political forces through democratic participation, noting that in the Middle East, when moderate Islamist parties have been allowed into the political process, support for extremist groups has declined. Aslan advocates for religious freedom and protection of religious minorities in the Middle East, calling on Iran to stop the "horrific human rights abuses" against its Baháʼí community and condemning the persecution and displacement of Middle Eastern Christian communities as a "regional religious cleansing" that will be a historic disaster for both Christians and Muslims. In a 2014 interview, he criticized "armchair atheism" among figures like Sam Harris and Bill Maher, who lack formal training in religion and thus cannot meaningfully discuss how religion influences human behavior, and he called Richard Dawkins a "buffoon, embarrassing himself every day," contrasting the New Atheists with earlier thinkers who were experts in religion and offered critiques grounded in education and research. On September 29, 2014, Antonia Blumberg of The Huffington Post reported that Aslan criticized Bill Maher for portraying female genital mutilation as an "Islamic problem" and for making sweeping generalizations about Islam, stating that equating Pakistan and Turkey as similar is "stupid," and he expressed broader concerns about how Muslims are portrayed in mainstream media. Prachi Gupta of Salon noted Aslan's claim that the U.S. was partnering with Saudi Arabia while condemning ISIS. In an October 8, 2014 article in The New York Times titled "Bill Maher Isn't the Only One Who Misunderstands Religion," Aslan argued that while Maher is right to condemn religious practices that violate human rights, failing to recognize religion's cultural embedding and making blanket judgments about Islam is bigotry. Eric Sasson of The New Republic challenged Aslan's claims that women are treated equally in Indonesia and Turkey due to elected female leaders, citing Human Rights Watch reports of a significant rollback of women's rights in both countries, and disputed his assertion that female genital mutilation is only a problem in central Africa, noting it also occurs in Malaysia. David Pakman also questioned some of Aslan's claims from the interview, and Sam Harris criticized Aslan for attributing violence in the Muslim world to individuals rather than Islam as a whole, calling his approach "post-modernist nonsense." Aslan and his former fiancée, journalist Amanda Fortini, ended their engagement in 2008. He married entrepreneur and author Jessica Jackley, a Christian, in 2011, forming an interfaith family with three sons. His aunt is the Iranian-American pop singer Leila Forouhar, and he is a fan of the professional football team the Las Vegas Raiders.
